A California Apple user has filed a lawsuit proposing a class action, accusing Apple of misleading customers about the privacy protection features of "Hide My Email." Below are the details of the incident.

Apple Sued Over Alleged Vulnerability in Hide My Email Feature

Recently, 404 Media reported that Apple was aware of a vulnerability that could expose the real email address behind a "Hide My Email" alias more than a year ago.

Apple's "Hide My Email" feature allows users to create unique, randomly generated email addresses and forward messages to their personal inbox, enabling them to sign up for apps, websites, and newsletters without revealing their real email address.

The feature is available for free through "Sign in with Apple," while a more comprehensive version is included in the iCloud+ plan, starting at US$0.99 per month, allowing users to create aliases for websites, newsletters, and other services.

According to 404 Media, a security researcher reported to Apple in June 2025 that a vulnerability could expose the real email address behind a "Hide My Email" alias.

Apple acknowledged receiving the report about a month later, but allegedly did not resolve the issue. In March 2026, Apple stated that the vulnerability had been fixed, but the researcher found that it could still be exploited.

404 Media reported as follows:

Back to the lawsuit (reported by MacRumors), the plaintiff Anthony Alvarez stated:

Apple was aware of the issue more than a year ago, but the vulnerability remains unfixed—during which time Apple continued to profit from "Hide My Email" and its privacy promises. The plaintiff is one of millions of customers who paid for iCloud+ and trusted Apple that "Hide My Email" would conceal their personal email address. The plaintiff and class members paid Apple for privacy protection—iCloud+ users through a premium included in the iCloud+ subscription fee, and all Apple customers through a premium included in Apple products, which Apple markets as offering

The lawsuit also notes that this is not an isolated case, citing a 2023 report that Apple's random MAC address feature could expose the user's real hardware identifier.

The complaint also claims that the total amount of claims for the proposed class exceeds US$5 million (excluding interest and litigation costs), but does not explain how that figure was calculated.

Alvarez, representing himself and other Apple customers he claims are similarly affected, has filed suit and is asking the court to certify the case as a class action, covering four proposed user groups:

  • Nationwide Apple customers who purchased a device and used the "Hide My Email" feature;
  • The California subset of the above users;
  • Nationwide iCloud+ subscribers who used the feature;
  • The California subset of iCloud+ subscribers.

He is requesting a jury trial and, in addition to unspecified monetary damages, is asking the court to order Apple to fix the "Hide My Email" feature or clearly disclose its limitations.

Apple has not yet responded to the lawsuit.
